# Email Plugin

SMTP email sending functionality for self-hosted Memos instances.

## Overview

This plugin provides a simple, reliable email sending interface following industry-standard SMTP protocols. It's designed for self-hosted environments where instance administrators configure their own email service, similar to platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Discourse.

## Features

- Standard SMTP protocol support
- TLS/STARTTLS and SSL/TLS encryption
- HTML and plain text emails
- Multiple recipients (To, Cc, Bcc)
- Synchronous and asynchronous sending
- Detailed error reporting with context
- Works with all major email providers
- Reply-To header support
- RFC 5322 compliant message formatting

## Quick Start

### 1. Configure SMTP Settings

```go
import "github.com/usememos/memos/internal/email"

config := &email.Config{
    SMTPHost:     "smtp.gmail.com",
    SMTPPort:     587,
    SMTPUsername: "your-email@gmail.com",
    SMTPPassword: "your-app-password",
    FromEmail:    "noreply@yourdomain.com",
    FromName:     "Memos",
    UseTLS:       true,
}
```

### 2. Create and Send Email

```go
message := &email.Message{
    To:      []string{"user@example.com"},
    Subject: "Welcome to Memos!",
    Body:    "Thanks for signing up.",
    IsHTML:  false,
}

// Synchronous send (waits for result)
err := email.Send(config, message)
if err != nil {
    log.Printf("Failed to send email: %v", err)
}

// Asynchronous send (returns immediately)
email.SendAsync(config, message)
```

## Provider Configuration

### Gmail

Requires an [App Password](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/185833) (2FA must be enabled):

```go
config := &email.Config{
    SMTPHost:     "smtp.gmail.com",
    SMTPPort:     587,
    SMTPUsername: "your-email@gmail.com",
    SMTPPassword: "your-16-char-app-password",
    FromEmail:    "your-email@gmail.com",
    FromName:     "Memos",
    UseTLS:       true,
}
```

**Alternative (SSL):**
```go
config := &email.Config{
    SMTPHost:     "smtp.gmail.com",
    SMTPPort:     465,
    SMTPUsername: "your-email@gmail.com",
    SMTPPassword: "your-16-char-app-password",
    FromEmail:    "your-email@gmail.com",
    FromName:     "Memos",
    UseSSL:       true,
}
```

### SendGrid

```go
config := &email.Config{
    SMTPHost:     "smtp.sendgrid.net",
    SMTPPort:     587,
    SMTPUsername: "apikey",
    SMTPPassword: "your-sendgrid-api-key",
    FromEmail:    "noreply@yourdomain.com",
    FromName:     "Memos",
    UseTLS:       true,
}
```

### AWS SES

```go
config := &email.Config{
    SMTPHost:     "email-smtp.us-east-1.amazonaws.com",
    SMTPPort:     587,
    SMTPUsername: "your-smtp-username",
    SMTPPassword: "your-smtp-password",
    FromEmail:    "verified@yourdomain.com",
    FromName:     "Memos",
    UseTLS:       true,
}
```

**Note:** Replace `us-east-1` with your AWS region. Email must be verified in SES.

No matches at all. This confirms there is no rate-limiting library dependency anywhere in the project (neither Go module nor npm package).

## Summary

**1. Does per-user API rate-limiting middleware exist? No.**

This is a Go backend (the "memos" self-hosted note app) using `echo` for HTTP and `connectrpc.com/connect` for its RPC API, with a React/Vite frontend under `web/`. I searched exhaustively for rate-limiting terminology (`rateLimit`, `rate-limit`, `throttle`, `express-rate-limit`, `limiter`, `RPM`, `quota`, HTTP 429/`TooManyRequests`) across:

- All server code (`server/`, `server/router/**`, `server/auth/`)
- Middleware/interceptor registration points (`server/server.go`, `server/router/api/v1/connect_interceptors.go`, `server/cors.go`)
- `internal/` packages, including `internal/scheduler/middleware.go` (this is job-scheduler middleware for background jobs, unrelated to HTTP/API requests)
- `internal/profile` (server config)
- Config files (`*.yaml`, `*.yml`, `*.json`)
- `go.mod`/`go.sum` for any Go rate-limiting library
- Frontend (`web/src`) and `web/package.json` / `web/pnpm-lock.yaml` for any npm rate-limit package

**Findings:**

- `server/server.go` (line 51-52) registers only two Echo middlewares: `middleware.Recover()` and a custom CORS middleware (`newCORSMiddleware`) — no rate limiting.
- `server/router/api/v1/connect_interceptors.go` defines four Connect-RPC interceptors: `MetadataInterceptor`, `LoggingInterceptor`, `RecoveryInterceptor`, and `AuthInterceptor` — none implement rate limiting or throttling.
- `go.mod` lists `golang.org/x/time v0.15.0` but only as an **indirect** (transitive) dependency; it is never imported anywhere in the codebase (`grep -rn "x/time/rate"` returns nothing), so it is not actually used for rate limiting.
- The only substantive mentions of "rate limit" in the repo are in `internal/email/README.md` (lines ~286-296) and `internal/email/doc.go` (line 86), where rate limiting is mentioned purely as a **suggested best practice / example code snippet** for administrators building on top of the email plugin (`limiter := rate.NewLimiter(rate.Every(time.Second), 10) // 10 emails per second`). This is documentation/example code only — it is not wired into the actual email-sending code path or any middleware/interceptor chain, and it has nothing to do with per-user API request rate-limiting.
- No `express-rate-limit`, `bottleneck`, or similar npm rate-limiting package appears in `web/package.json` or `web/pnpm-lock.yaml`.

**2. File paths:** Not applicable — no such middleware is defined or registered anywhere.

**3. Limit numbers/config:** Not applicable, except the illustrative (non-functional) example in `internal/email/README.md` line 292: `rate.NewLimiter(rate.Every(time.Second), 10) // 10 emails per second` — this is documentation prose, not live code.

**Conclusion:** After a thorough search, this codebase contains no implemented per-user (or any other) API rate-limiting/throttling middleware. The only related content is an illustrative code snippet in email plugin documentation recommending that *administrators* consider adding rate limiting for outbound email sending — it is not implemented or registered anywhere in the request-handling pipeline.
